newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo central bank bonds rate hits record high.
newsitem.headline: Yugo central bank bonds rate hits record high.

text.p: The Yugoslav Central Bank set a record high interest rate for its short term bonds auctioned on Monday, raising the rate to an annual 122.29 percent, the Belgrade bourse said.
This compares to the 115.61 percent interest rate set for the previous tranche of bonds, and the lowest rate ever on those securities of 60.7 percent.
National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) auctioned the new 50 million dinar ($9.89 million) tranche of its 30-day bonds but sold only three million dinars worth, the bourse said.
"The sale results show that we may have wrongly timed this auction because market liquidity is tight," a central bank official said.
Market liquidity drastically deteriorated in mid-September when the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) introduced a 10 percent reserve requirement.

"Since then, commercial banks have set aside almost 270 million dinars for the reserve requirement. But along with that, market liquidity was marred by the usual withdrawal of funds to pay salaries and pensions," head of the NBY open market operations department Voja Scekic told Reuters.
According to Scekic, the banks' attitude towards the NBY's short-term bonds directly reflected the reserve requirement.
In June, NBY made a fruitless effort to influence other interest rates by gradually lowering rates on its short-term bonds and extending the paper's maturity to 60 days.
Two months later, the central bank decided to restore the old shine on its instrument, first launched late last November to control market liquidity.
Rates on short-term bonds resumed their upward trend at the end of August, when the NBY decided to minimise the influence of the bonds on its discount rate policy.

"We have noticed an improved liquidity among banks and were afraid it could spill over elsewhere. So we could not take a chance and decided to attract money again in our bonds," the NBY vice-governor Ratko Banovic said, saying there were no other reasons for higher interest rate on those bonds. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
